doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: The Newport panel and leaving DownBeat
summary: He recounts leaving DownBeat over trouble with the publisher and being attacked on a Newport panel with Max Roach, who later told him it was not personal.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: there was — Newport in New York had, in the beginning, in their earlier years, they had some side events, panel discussions and stuff. And I was invited — this was just around the time when I was leaving DownBeat because I had real problems with the publisher, who was the son of the original publisher, old man Maher, who had his quirks but I was able to get along with him and you knew where he was coming from. His son was really somebody who came in without having any experience with or knowledge of jazz other than what he had absorbed from the family. And he and his father didn’t get along at all so it was a shortcut there too. But I just had to leave the magazine. It was right in the middle of that, which of course nobody outside was really aware of other than people close to me, and I was asked to be on this panel. I think it was called “The Drum” or something or other. It turned out that I was the only white person along with about five guys who were — some of them were educators — I didn’t even know most of them — and Max Roach, who was the moderator. And some of the people on there were very much to the left. And I was raked over the coals, not only as representing DownBeat, that’s one thing, but then it also became — you know there were racial matters that came into it. And I finally said something about, you know, I’d had enough of this. And it wasn’t easy. And in the audience there were also some people who chimed in on that. There were actually some people in Newark, where I hadn’t been yet because it was before — I wasn’t with the Institute yet. Anyway, I finally made a little speech and I walked out, and walked off. But that was after some considerable time. So anyway, the first person to come out and join me in the hallway was Martin Williams, you know, we were friends and he hugged me and he said — but then when it was over, I still — I didn’t go away, I stayed. I think there was something going on after that that I wanted to attend. And then Max came out. And Max and I were old acquaintances. I wouldn’t say that we were close friends but we were certainly well acquainted. And then Max came over and he actually gave me a hug too and then he said something interesting, he said, “You have to understand,” he said, “this wasn’t personal.” He said, “This is something that we have to go through.”
